summary: Lists the requirements for several common IPsec remote access scenarios, which share some needs and differ in others. A thorough understanding of them is needed to judge which mechanisms suit each case. It is informational and sets the stage for later work.

eli5.summary: People connect to work from home, hotels and cafes, and each situation needs different things. This note lists those needs so solutions can be judged fairly.

subtitle: Security requirements for different ways employees and partners access corporate networks.

tldr.problem: Remote access—employees connecting from home, hotels, and public WiFi—requires security, but each scenario has different risks, trust levels, and technical constraints. One solution does not fit all.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies five common remote access scenarios (telecommuters, corporate extranets, visiting employees, borrowed systems) and specifies requirements in five areas for each: endpoint authentication (who is connecting), device configuration (network setup for the remote host), security policy (what traffic is allowed), auditing (who connected when), and intermediary traversal (passing through firewalls and NAT devices).
tldr.outcome: The document enabled protocol designers and implementers to understand what mechanisms are needed for each scenario and to evaluate whether specific IPsec proposals suit particular deployment patterns, rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all solution.

facts.label: Requirement categories
facts.value: 5 (authentication, device config, policy, auditing, intermediary traversal)

today: RFC 3457 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains a comprehensive reference for understanding the security and operational requirements of different remote access scenarios. While specific IPsec mechanisms have evolved since 2003 (particularly with the development of newer IKE versions and mobility protocols), the fundamental scenario-specific requirements outlined in this document continue to inform secure remote access deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Common Requirements
sections.content:
IPsec provides strong cryptographic security for remote access, but deploying it securely requires careful attention to several categories of requirements. All secure remote access scenarios share a common high-level structure: a remote client (IRAC) connects securely through the Internet to a security gateway or host (IRAS/SGW) protecting the target network. However, the details—who is trusted, what devices are involved, and what connectivity constraints exist—vary widely.

This document does not propose specific solutions but enumerates requirements across five common scenarios. The five requirement categories are: endpoint authentication (verifying the identity of the client and server), remote host configuration (assigning the client a network address and other settings), security policy configuration (controlling what traffic is allowed), auditing (logging connections for security and compliance), and intermediary traversal (passing through firewalls and NAT boxes).
sections.eli5: Remote connections need security, but the details depend on the situation. This part explains the five areas that every remote access scenario must address.

sections.title: Endpoint Authentication Challenges
sections.content:
Machine-level authentication verifies the identity of the device (stored credentials, smartcard, or certificate) without requiring user input. This is simple and persistent but does not confirm the user is authorized to use the device. User-level authentication requires the user to provide something (password, one-time code, smartcard PIN), confirming the user is present. Combined authentication uses both: a machine credential (stronger than a password) combined with user input (ensuring the user is at the device).

In remote access, server authentication is usually straightforward—the client needs to verify it is connecting to the real company server, not an imposter. Client authentication is harder. For at-risk scenarios (traveling users, publicly borrowed systems), periodic renewal of user authentication is important to prevent unauthorized use of an unattended device. The RFC acknowledges that no solution is foolproof when the client device itself may be compromised by malware.
sections.eli5: Three levels of ID checking exist: proving a device is authentic (like a key card), proving a person is authentic (like a password), or both. Each situation needs different strength and frequency of checking.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Telecommuters (Dialup/DSL/Cable)
sections.content:
A common scenario is an employee at home or in a hotel connecting via dialup, DSL, or cable modem. The client receives an IP address from the ISP (either dynamically each time or statically if using DSL/cable). The remote client must authenticate to the company's security gateway, and the gateway must authenticate to the client (so the client knows it is not connected to a fake gateway).

The gateway MUST provide machine-level authentication; the client SHOULD support user authentication, and if protection against unauthorized use is desired, the client MUST provide it (with periodic renewal for always-on connections). The client typically needs a virtual IP address from the corporate network so it appears to be on the corporate LAN, enabling it to receive subnet broadcasts and use NetBIOS, WINS, and other LAN services. The client SHOULD support policy configuration to block Internet traffic during the tunnel (or force it through the tunnel), and the gateway MAY support dynamic policy updates. For intermediary traversal, if the ISP uses NAPT (network address translation), a mechanism is needed to pass IPsec through it.
sections.eli5: An employee dials in from home. The company server proves it is real, the employee proves they are the real employee, and the employee's computer gets a temporary address that makes it look like it is in the office. Firewalls between the employee and the company must not block the encrypted tunnel.

sections.title: Scenario 2: Corporate Extranets and Site-to-Site
sections.content:
In an extranet, a user from one corporation accesses resources on another corporation's network. The two companies have a business relationship but do not fully trust each other. Authentication requirements depend on whether all employees of Company A are allowed, or only a specific user. For per-user access control, user-level authentication is required; machine authentication might suffice if the organizational unit is physically secure.

Device configuration requirements are lighter than for telecommuters—a virtual address might not be needed, or the benefits might be unclear. Policy configuration is mostly static (allowing traffic between the user and specific target servers) unless dynamic updates based on the authenticated user's identity are implemented. Intermediary traversal requirements are similar to telecommuters: if NAT or a firewall blocks IPsec, mechanisms are needed to work around it.
sections.eli5: An employee from Company A wants to access a server at Company B. Both companies need to verify who is connecting and what they are allowed to access, but the trust is limited to specific resources, not the entire network.

sections.title: Scenarios 3 & 4: Visiting Employees (Laptop and Desktop)
sections.content:
When a Company A employee travels to Company B's office to work, they bring their laptop or use a desktop at Company B. This is higher-risk than a telecommuter because the device is on a foreign network and may be unattended. User-level authentication SHOULD be provided in addition to (or instead of) machine-level authentication, and periodic renewal of user authentication MUST occur to guard against unauthorized use of an unattended system.

A laptop scenario adds a complication: the laptop has an address on Company B's network and may need to access Company B's resources, while still accessing Company A's resources through the tunnel. Internet-bound traffic should not be forced through the tunnel, but other traffic might be blocked or restricted. For a desktop (Company A has no control over), restrictions are even lighter—Company A cannot easily enforce policies on a foreign machine it does not own. Both scenarios require detecting and logging when connections start and end.
sections.eli5: When visiting another office, an employee's laptop needs stronger identification (periodic password checks) because no one knows if the person who walked away is the person who will come back. And the laptop might be used to access the visitor's office too, which complicates routing.

sections.title: Scenario 5: Public Systems (Airport Kiosk)
sections.content:
The highest-risk scenario is using a public system the company does not own or trust. Machine authentication is meaningless—the company cannot verify the kiosk is authentic or uncompromised. User-level authentication MUST be provided, but a static password is extremely risky because the kiosk may capture it. A one-time password mitigates this somewhat, but if the kiosk is actively malicious, it may capture the one-time code and use it before the user does, or it may have already captured IPsec keys. In untrusted scenarios, sensitive data SHOULD NOT be transmitted.

In this scenario, there are no device configuration or policy configuration requirements—the company cannot control or trust the foreign device. The client should at least authenticate the server (with a certificate or pre-shared knowledge) to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker intercepts the connection and captures credentials. Connection auditing is still required to log that someone connected.
sections.eli5: Using a computer in an airport or library to access work email is extremely risky because the computer itself might be malicious. The company cannot rely on device-level protections; the employee must verify the company's server is real, and should only access non-sensitive data.
